vignette: A 21-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted for bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension, meaning her blood pressure drops when she stands. She is eating only about 25% of her meals and refuses oral nutritional supplements. Her QTc interval is normal at 420 ms, indicating a stable heart rhythm. Her abdomen is distended with absent bowel sounds, and she has had two episodes of vomiting today. She agrees to “try harder tomorrow,” but her intake has not improved over 24 hours, and her weight has been stable since admission.

excerpt.text:
She is eating only about a quarter of her meals and refuses oral supplements, and neither has improved since yesterday. Her weight has been stable and her QTc is normal, so another day of watching is not an unreasonable hope. She agrees to try harder tomorrow, and a feeding tube would go against a preference she is stating in plain words.

Continued monitoring is the choice that respects what she is asking. It also leaves the intake where it is. She was admitted for bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension, and a stable weight on this little food is not the same as the deficit turning around.

A feeding tube would replace what she is not taking, and it would override her. Her abdomen is distended, bowel sounds are absent, and she has vomited twice today, which makes me less willing to count on tomorrow. Her rhythm is stable enough that the question is the nutrition, not an emergency around the procedure.

I would place the feeding tube rather than continue monitoring.

recommendation.text: I would place the feeding tube rather than continue monitoring.
